extracted.intended_audience: general public, policymakers, transparency and civil‑liberties advocates interested in national security law and government accountability
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion/analysis arguing that legally binding rules, interpretations, and directives that affect citizens should be public and subject to democratic oversight. The piece identifies sources of 'secret law' in national security and recommends disclosure and publication reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability of law and legal analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: A growing body of 'secret law' enacted without public scrutiny or Congressional input poses a threat to the functioning of our democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law and legal analyses that govern public action should be available to the public and subject to Congressional input; withholding authoritative legal opinions or interpretations (e.g., those justifying surveillance or interrogation practices) undermines democratic accountability. Examples: OLC 'torture memos' and legal analyses authorizing warrantless wiretapping were withheld yet later judged illegal. Anti-pattern: treating binding legal interpretations as permanently classified and inaccessible to public or legislative oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of agency rules and regulations (Federal Register requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence agencies routinely issue rules and regulations without publishing them in the Federal Register, exploiting what are intended to be narrow exceptions to the publication requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should publish binding rules and regulations in the Federal Register except where truly narrow, statutorily authorized exemptions apply. Exploiting exceptions to avoid publication is a misuse that produces secret binding rules. Example: intelligence agency rules not published; remedy: enforce publication obligations and tighten exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of judicial interpretations that alter statutory meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: When the FISA court construed the Patriot Act to allow bulk collection of Americans’ phone records, that interpretation became part of the statute’s meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court interpretations that materially affect the meaning or application of statutes — especially secretive panels like the FISA court — should be made public or subject to rigorous oversight, because concealed interpretations effectively change how statutes operate. Anti-pattern: treating court opinions that expand executive power as secret and binding without public disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of presidential directives on national security
rubrics_metrics.description: Most presidential directives addressing national security policy are not made public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presidential directives that set procedures and standards (for example, on use of lethal force or detention policy) should be disclosed when they have binding effect on agency conduct, or otherwise be subject to appropriate oversight, so the public and Congress can assess policy and legality. Anti-pattern: issuing broad executive directives in secret and binding officials without public accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of binding international agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents released by the State Department in litigation reveal that 42 percent of binding agreements between the United States and other countries are unpublished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binding agreements that constrain U.S. government action toward foreign states or persons should be published or otherwise made accessible, because unpublished international commitments can hide material legal obligations. Example: high percentage of unpublished agreements found in State Department records. Remedy: increase publication and transparency of such agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declassification and release of Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) opinions on national security
rubrics_metrics.description: At least 74 O.L.C. opinions from 2002 to 2009 on national security issues remain classified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OLC opinions that provide the legal basis for controversial or consequential national security programs should be declassified or summarized to the extent possible so the public and Congress can evaluate legality and policy. Anti-pattern: retaining broad swaths of OLC national security opinions in permanent secrecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release of significant FISA court opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite disclosure of many FISA court opinions following Edward Snowden’s revelations, new information from the Justice Department indicates that about 30 significant opinions remain secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant FISA court opinions — particularly those that authorize expansive surveillance practices — should be disclosed (fully or in redacted form) to permit public understanding and oversight. Anti-pattern: keeping important judicial rulings that shape surveillance law permanently sealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit and narrow secrecy exceptions to protect democratic functioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Secret law persists through agencies exploiting narrow exceptions and through institutional practices that keep binding legal material hidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secrecy exceptions should be tightly construed and narrowly applied; institutional practices that allow routine withholding of binding legal materials must be reformed to ensure transparency. Example remedies: stricter interpretation of publication exemptions, proactive disclosure policies. Anti-pattern: broad administrative interpretations of 'exception' that swallow publication requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency as a democratic safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: Informed citizens are democracy’s best defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency in government lawmaking, legal interpretations, and policy formation is a core democratic value — lack of transparency (secret law) threatens democratic governance. This normative standard underpins calls for publication, disclosure, oversight, and reform. Application: prioritize disclosure policies where secrecy impedes public debate and Congressional oversight.
